profiles.meeting_scenario: An internal design review at a diversified chemicals company for a proposed stage-gate assessment framework that links Technology Readiness Levels (TRLs) to techno-economic assessment (TEA) methods for low-carbon process concepts. The draft framework will be used by R&D, process development, and corporate investment teams to review projects such as electrified cracking add-ons, CO2-derived intermediates, and solvent recycling technologies before the next portfolio round. The agenda is to review whether the framework's TRL definitions, cost-estimation ladder, and profitability indicators are practical and sufficiently consistent for real project reviews, and to decide whether it can be approved for pilot use with minor edits. The expected outcome is a go/no-go on adopting the framework for the upcoming Q3 stage-gate cycle, plus a short list of revisions to the draft.

members.name: Dr. Lena Vogt
members.expertise: Process modeling, scale-up economics, pilot-to-commercial TEA in chemical manufacturing
members.background: Chemical engineer who spent eight years in process development and pilot campaigns before moving into central innovation to standardize TEA practices across early-stage RD&D programs.
members.private_state: She wants the framework approved quickly so R&D teams can use it without needing finance-grade inputs too early; she is concerned that if the framework becomes too burdensome, project teams will bypass it or populate it with low-quality placeholder numbers.
hidden_assumptions: TRL labels in this framework should primarily reflect technical evidence quality, especially whether mass and energy balances are experimentally grounded.
The phrase 'validated data' mainly refers to experimentally reconciled process data, not commercial or procurement validation.
At early and mid TRLs, 'installed CAPEX' can reasonably stop at process-unit and direct/indirect installation costs, with broader site and owner costs added later.
A required 'sensitivity analysis' for early TRLs should be lightweight and local, using one-variable changes around a base case to expose process levers.

members.name: Arun Mehta
members.expertise: Capital review, portfolio comparison, business-case standardization for industrial projects
members.background: Former petrochemicals project controller who now supports the investment committee by translating technical project cases into comparable capital allocation decisions across business units.
members.private_state: He wants the framework to map cleanly into the investment committee's templates so projects at different maturity levels can still be compared on a common basis; he is concerned that technically elegant but nonstandard analyses will create inconsistency across the portfolio.
hidden_assumptions: TRL labels are only useful internally if they also signal what level of decision readiness a project has for funding gates.
The phrase 'validated data' should include commercially grounded inputs such as budgetary quotes, utility-price assumptions, and credible operating-cost ranges.
For portfolio comparison, 'installed CAPEX' should already include typical OSBL, EPCM, owner's cost, and commissioning allowances rather than stopping at process units.
A required 'sensitivity analysis' should follow the corporate scenario package, with linked movements in electricity price, carbon price, discount rate, and subsidy assumptions.

misalignment_points.topic: Meaning of 'validated data' at the TRL transition
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to needing 'validated data' before the framework shifts from static indicators to more detailed economic treatment around TRL 5.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means experimentally validated process data: closed mass/energy balances from integrated runs, measured yields, and engineering assumptions anchored in pilot evidence.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means decision-validated business inputs: sufficiently credible commercial assumptions, budgetary price inputs, and vendor-backed ranges that can support an investment-style model.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is standard in both technical and finance contexts, and both interpretations sound reasonable within a design review; each person hears a familiar domain meaning and sees no immediate reason to unpack it.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss the framework's 'installed CAPEX' field as the capital basis used across TRLs.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes it mainly covers inside-battery-limits process equipment plus installation factors and process contingency, with broader site infrastructure and owner-side costs layered in later when the project matures.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes it already includes a fuller project-capital envelope suitable for comparison across opportunities, including OSBL utilities, EPCM, commissioning, and owner's costs via standard uplifts.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In industrial practice, both narrower and broader cost boundaries are routinely labeled 'installed CAPEX,' and the difference is often buried in spreadsheet conventions rather than spoken aloud in meetings.

misalignment_points.topic: How the required 'sensitivity analysis' will be run
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that every TRL stage in the framework should include a 'sensitivity analysis.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes a simple one-at-a-time analysis on a few technical levers such as yield, selectivity, uptime, and electricity price, mainly to show directional drivers when data are sparse.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the standard corporate scenario set will be used, with correlated shifts across power prices, carbon costs, discount rates, financing assumptions, and policy support.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Sensitivity analysis is treated as a routine hygiene item rather than a design choice, so both participants naturally endorse it without clarifying the method because the surface agreement feels complete.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to get approved with only light edits. If we burden early R&D teams with finance-grade detail, they'll either dodge the framework or fill it with junk assumptions. The draft is intentionally practical: simple technical screens first, then more structured TEA as the evidence base improves.
turns.utterance: Thanks, everyone. The main goal today is just to make sure this TRL-linked TEA framework is usable for the Q3 portfolio cycle. The draft already ties the readiness bands to the cost ladder and the profitability views, so what I'd like from this review is a final check that it's practical in real project discussions and not asking teams for more than they can credibly provide at each stage.

turns.inner_thought: Usable is fine, but only if it lands cleanly in the investment committee process. I do not want another technically interesting framework that produces cases finance has to rebuild from scratch to compare across business units. Early-stage should stay lean, but the outputs still need to line up with funding gates.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. From my side, I mainly want to confirm that it will behave consistently in stage-gate decisions across very different project types without turning the early cases into mini-FEED studies. If we can keep it proportionate but still comparable, that's a good outcome.

turns.inner_thought: At the lower TRLs, teams should stay with static indicators until they have experimentally reconciled balances and pilot-grounded assumptions. That's what validated data means here to me. Once the process evidence is real, we can justify moving beyond rough screening without pretending the economics are firmer than the science.
turns.utterance: Right, and that's exactly why the framework keeps the lower bands on static indicators and only shifts into more detailed economics once there is enough validated data around the mid-readiness stages. That transition point is there to avoid false precision while still giving teams a clear path forward.

turns.inner_thought: Good. Once they have validated data, I would expect the commercial assumptions to be credible enough for committee use: budgetary inputs, grounded ranges, something we can defend in a funding packet. If that threshold is built in, the later-stage cases should slot into our templates without drama.
turns.utterance: Yes, I like that breakpoint. Once validated data are in place, the case should be robust enough to flow into the committee packet with a more decision-grade economic view. That gives people a sensible distinction between exploratory work and something that can support an actual funding discussion.

turns.inner_thought: The capital ladder is deliberately simple early on. Installed CAPEX should give teams a stable basis centered on the process scope, then we can broaden later as projects mature. If we force full project-cost framing too soon, people will spend weeks inventing numbers for things they don't yet understand.
turns.utterance: On the costing side, the ladder is meant to be straightforward. The installed CAPEX field gives a clean basis for comparing concepts as they move from rough factors toward better estimates, and it lets us keep a common capital reference across the TRLs rather than changing the headline metric every time the case matures.

turns.inner_thought: Exactly. If installed CAPEX is the common basis, then we can compare opportunities without later discovering one case includes the broader project envelope and another doesn't. This should reduce the rework we usually do when we add OSBL, EPCM, owner's costs, commissioning, and all the standard uplifts before portfolio review.
turns.utterance: Agreed. Using installed CAPEX as the common capital basis should help a lot with comparability across projects, and ideally it means finance doesn't have to keep reworking cases later just to make them line up for portfolio review. That consistency matters more than having a different costing language in every program.

turns.inner_thought: I also need to reassure people that uncertainty is handled without making early teams build giant scenario packs. A compact sensitivity analysis is enough to show which technical levers matter when data are sparse. The point is directionality, not a full corporate risk model at TRL 3 or 4.
turns.utterance: The other piece I think is important is that each TRL band includes a compact sensitivity analysis. That way teams can still show what is driving the economics even when the underlying data are thin, and reviewers can see whether the conclusion is stable or hanging on one or two assumptions.

turns.inner_thought: Good, because I want the sensitivity analysis to mesh with the corporate scenario package. If we can roll the same structure into planning assumptions on power, carbon, discounting, and policy support, then the portfolio team can compare exposures without inventing a new method case by case.
turns.utterance: I agree, that's essential. The same sensitivity analysis should also roll neatly into the planning scenarios the portfolio team uses for carbon and power exposure, so we're not treating uncertainty one way in R&D reviews and another way when the portfolio gets consolidated.

turns.inner_thought: The appendix examples are there to show exactly that progression: from simple screening based on experimentally grounded process evidence, through a manageable installed CAPEX view, and a lightweight sensitivity analysis, then later into fuller dynamic cases. I just need Arun comfortable enough not to reopen the whole architecture.
turns.utterance: If you look at the appendix examples, I think they show the scaling pretty well. The framework starts with rough screening, then moves into more developed cases as the project matures, but without forcing unrealistic detail too early. So across validated data, installed CAPEX, and the sensitivity analysis, the progression is there without making the front end too heavy.

turns.inner_thought: This is close enough to workable. I still assume the later-stage definitions will naturally support committee-ready inputs, and if needed we can tidy wording after pilot use. Better to get it into Q3 now and normalize teams onto one format than keep debating details for another quarter.
turns.utterance: From my side, this is basically ready for pilot adoption. I would suggest only a few wording cleanups before it goes into the Q3 review package, mainly so the transition around validated data reads clearly and the framework comes across as one consistent standard from early screening through later gate reviews.
